title: Quantifying CO 2 Green House Gas Emissions from Soil Dredging in Drainage Basin of River Niger at Otu Ogwu Asaba
abstract: CO 2 otherwise carbon-dioxide, is a gas of colourless form comprising of a single carbon and two atoms of oxygen, bonded through reaction. Carbon dioxide status obtainable through appropriate quantification is of importance to agriculture, climate change, human health concerns, etc. Objectively, this work summarily point on "Quantifying CO 2 green house gas emissions from soil dredging in drainage basin of River Niger at Otu Ogwu Asaba". In this work, a one year measurement involving field survey, data generation, computations and documentation, with respect to energy consumption by aquatic equipment operations relative to soil dredging which requires burning of diesel and petrol fuels, potentially contributing to atmospheric emittable greenhouse gases of which carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) was primarily focused on. Conclusively, 3,736.03 Kg CO₂e, and 44,832.32 Kg CO₂e, of average and total CO₂ otherwise carbon - dioxid emissions were attributed to the area in general. Also, 1403.64 Kg CO₂e, and, 5565.54 Kg CO₂e, of minimal and maximal CO 2 emissions occurred at the area, in the months of July (medium) and December (high) respectively. Moreso, the diesel energy consumption outweighed petrol with respect to their contribution to CO 2 emissions to the environment. While balance in environmental emissions were maintained by changing yieldings of low, medium and high CO 2 input from human activities as well as atmospheric air mixtures.
authors: G. Okolotu, R. Nwadiolu, O. Akwenuke, C. Okeke

title: Divergent methane production and microbial community responses to carbon enrichment in freshwater wetland sediments
authors: Julia Ghantous, Hassan Azaizah, Elad Levintal, Rotem Golan, Y. Rosenberg, G. Antler, K. Yanuka-Golub

title: Magnitudes of carbon sequestration offsets by CH4 emission in restored Kandelia obovata mangrove ecosystems in a subtropical estuary.
abstract: Mangrove forests can absorb and store atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) over long timescales within their soils and vegetation. However, soil organic carbon in mangrove ecosystems can be mineralized and released to the atmosphere as methane (CH4), a greenhouse gas with a much higher global warming potential than CO2. As a result, CH4 emissions can partially offset net ecosystem CO2 uptake. In this study, we quantified the annual plant biomass carbon increment, sediment carbon burial, and temporal variations of CH4 emissions from three interfaces-sediment-atmosphere, water-atmosphere, and plant-atmosphere in the restored Kandelia obovata mangrove forest in the Minjiang River estuary, China. CH4 fluxes at the sediment-atmosphere interface were 2.5 times higher than those at the water-atmosphere interface, and ebullition was the dominant CH4 emissions pathway at the water-atmosphere interface. The annual mean CH4 flux from the restored K. obovata mangrove forest ecosystem was 2.19±0.22 mg·m-2 h-1. Over the annual scale, the relative surface elevation of the restored mangrove forest increased by 32.7± 2.16 mm. The ecosystem carbon sink rate was 4384.5±622.4 g CO2-eq m-2 a-1. CH4 emission offset 10.5% of the net carbon fixation of mangrove vegetation and 26.0% of the sediment carbon burial rate. Our findings indicate that although CH4 emissions partially offset net carbon sequestration capacity of restored mangrove forests, restored mangrove stands still function as substantial net greenhouse gas sinks over a 100-year time horizon. Protecting and restoring mangrove carbon stocks is therefore an important component of global climate change mitigation strategies.
authors: Chuan Tong, Zhi-Hua Feng, Yi-Xuan Yu, Zhong-Hao Ding, Jia-Fang Huang, Yang Ping, Min-Jie Hu, Wen-Bo Lin

title: Seasonally shifting methane-control regimes across urban rivers and urban wetland rivers in the GBA, China, revealed by environmental, isotopic, and microbial evidence.
abstract: Urban rivers (UR) and urban wetland rivers (WR) are increasingly recognized as CH4 sources, yet the processes underlying differences between these aquatic habitats remain poorly resolved. We investigated excess CH4 concentration (ΔCH4), estimated diffusive flux, environmental conditions, stable carbon isotopes, and sediment microbial functional potential in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA), China. CH4 dynamics exhibited a clear seasonal shift between contrasting spatial patterns. UR showed an amplified CH4 state during the first two seasons, the wetland outlet (WO) in wet season 1 and than both WR and WO in dry season 1. In UR, ΔCH4 decreased with dissolved oxygen (β = -0.194, p = 0.020) and increased with total nitrogen (β = 0.272, p = 0.003), indicating strong nutrient-redox control on CH4 accumulation. Stable-isotope signatures overlapped broadly among potential production and oxidation processes, while WR displayed more 13C-depleted CH4 than UR during wet season 1 despite lower ΔCH4, indicating that source signatures did not translate directly into net CH4 accumulation. Consistently, mcr and CO2-reducing methanogenesis genes and methanogenic taxa were relatively enriched in early UR seasons, whereas pmo-family genes and methane-oxidizing taxa were distributed more broadly across WR and WO. Together, these complementary lines of evidence reveal a seasonally reversible transition from nutrient-redox-driven CH4 amplification in urban rivers to more complex wetland-associated regulation involving carbon supply, redox heterogeneity, and methane-oxidation potential.
authors: Hai-Guang Qin, Si-Bo Zhang, Fei-Yang Xia, Qian Tan, Hang Wan, Yan-Peng Cai

title: Constraining combustion efficiency and CO to CO2 emission ratio in the Yangtze River Delta region by using high-altitude atmospheric observations
